abstract: Habitat selection is a fundamentally hierarchical process implying that choices made by animals at broad spatial scales constrain those made at finer ones. How selection for the same habitats relates across hierarchical orders remains largely untested empirically. We investigated whether selection for a given habitat at the larger scale reinforces itself, is independent of, or opposes selection for the same habitat at the finer scale. Using GPS-collared European hares (Lepus europaeus, n = 52) in a mid-mountain grassland landscape (French Jura, 2021-2023), we jointly quantified and compared temporal variation in second-order (home range placement within the landscape) and third-order (habitat use within home ranges) selection with generalised linear mixed models, and resource selection functions. The association in selection strength between orders was strongly habitat-dependent: significantly positive for grasslands, forests and farm tracks, but negative for fodder crops. Our results suggest that hierarchical levels of habitat selection can couple or decouple depending on the habitat considered and what resources European hares are seeking at the different scales. Temporal variability in selection was consistently greater within home ranges than at the landscape level, and seasonal variation in ecological conditions (temperature, precipitation) shaped fine-scale selection while leaving landscape-level selection largely unaffected. Large-scale selection by European hare appeared relatively stable over time while fine-scale selection allowed dynamic behavioural adjustments to short-term variability of environmental conditions. Our results illustrate a hierarchical strategy of stable placement of the home range, flexible use within it. Reliance on heterogeneous open and semi-open habitats and consistent avoidance of built-up areas also clarifies the habitat requirements of the European hare in grassland-dominated agricultural landscapes, given population declines across much of its native range.
